code.title: Fibonacci: plain recursion vs a memo (count the calls)
code.python:
calls = 0
memo = {}


# Plain recursion: the same subproblem is solved again and again.
def naive(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return naive(n - 1) + naive(n - 2)


# DP (memoization): solve each n once, store it, reuse it.
def fast(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n < 2:
        return n
    if n in memo:            # already solved: reuse
        return memo[n]
    memo[n] = fast(n - 1) + fast(n - 2)
    return memo[n]


n = 30
print("n =", n)
calls = 0
a = naive(n)
print("plain recursion: fib = " + str(a) + ", calls = " + str(calls))
calls = 0
b = fast(n)
print("with a memo:     fib = " + str(b) + ", calls = " + str(calls))
# Time: about 1.6^n calls without the memo, O(n) with it. Space: O(n).

followUps:
Both split a problem into smaller ones, but in divide & conquer the smaller problems are all different, while in DP the same ones come up again and again, so DP saves their answers.

Merge sort on 8 numbers sorts the left 4 and the right 4. Those halves share nothing, so no piece is ever sorted twice and a cache would stay unused. In fib(5) the call fib(3) appears 2 times and fib(2) 3 times, so storing each answer once cuts the work from about 1.6n calls to O(n).

Quick test: draw the recursion tree. If a node repeats, it is DP. If every node is unique, plain recursion is already as fast as it gets.

Greedy makes one choice at each step and never looks back; DP tries every choice and keeps the best, so DP is slower but safe.

Take coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6. Greedy grabs 4 first and is then stuck with 1 + 1, giving 3 coins. DP compares all last coins: dp[6] = 1 + min(dp[5], dp[3], dp[2]) = 1 + min(2, 1, 2) = 2, which is 3 + 3.

Greedy needs a proof that the local best choice is always part of some best full answer (interval scheduling by earliest end time has one). When that proof exists, greedy usually costs O(n log n) for a sort and O(1) extra space. DP costs states × choices, here O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) space.

code.title: Fewest coins: top-down memoization vs bottom-up tabulation
code.python:
coins = [5, 10, 25]
INF = 1000000
amount = 100
memo = [-1] * (amount + 1)
solved = 0


# Top-down: recursion + cache. It only visits amounts it can actually reach.
def best(a):
    global solved
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    if a < 0:
        return INF
    if memo[a] != -1:
        return memo[a]
    solved += 1
    res = INF
    for c in coins:
        res = min(res, 1 + best(a - c))
    memo[a] = res
    return res


print("coins = [5, 10, 25], amount = " + str(amount))
top = best(amount)
print("top-down  (memoization): fewest coins = " + str(top) + ", states solved = " + str(solved))

# Bottom-up: a loop fills every amount from 1 to 100 in order.
dp = [0] * (amount + 1)
filled = 0
for a in range(1, amount + 1):
    dp[a] = INF
    for c in coins:
        if a >= c:
            dp[a] = min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - c])
    filled += 1
print("bottom-up (tabulation):  fewest coins = " + str(dp[amount]) + ", states solved = " + str(filled))
# Both: O(amount * coins) time worst case, O(amount) space.
# Top-down also uses the call stack; bottom-up uses no recursion.

followUps:
Top-down wins outright when only a small part of the table is ever needed, or when the fill order is hard to write as loops.

  • Sparse states. With coins {5, 10, 25} and amount 100, recursion visits only the 20 multiples of 5; a loop fills all 100 cells. If the amount were 109 and each step halves it, a hash-map memo touches about 30 states, while a table cannot even be allocated.
  • Awkward order. DP on a tree, a DAG or game positions: recursion follows the dependencies for you, so you do not need a topological order first.

The cost is the same per state, O(states × work per state), plus hash-map and call overhead.

The sure fix is to stop recursing: rewrite the DP bottom-up with loops, so the depth is 0 no matter how large n is.

If you must keep the recursion:

  • Python: the default limit is about 1000 frames. Raise it with sys.setrecursionlimit(300000) and run the solver in a thread after threading.stack_size(256 * 1024 * 1024).
  • Java: run the solver in new Thread(null, task, "dp", 1L << 28) to get a 256 MB stack.
  • JS: no reliable switch, so use loops or your own stack array.
  • C++ / C#: the stack is 1 to 8 MB, good for roughly 104 to 105 frames; beyond that use loops.

Example: climb(100000) top-down needs 100000 frames; the loop version needs 2 variables.

code.title: The five DP design steps on House Robber
code.python:
# House Robber: pick houses with the largest total, never two neighbours.
money = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
n = len(money)
print("money = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]")

# Step 1 (state): dp[i] = most money using only the first i houses.
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
# Step 3 (base cases): no houses -> 0, one house -> take it.
dp[0] = 0
dp[1] = money[0]
# Step 4 (order): left to right, so dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] are ready.
for i in range(2, n + 1):
    # Step 2 (transition): last decision = skip house i, or rob it.
    dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + money[i - 1])

print("dp    = " + " ".join(str(x) for x in dp))
# Step 5 (answer location): dp[n].
print("answer = dp[" + str(n) + "] = " + str(dp[n]))
# Cost = states * work per state = n * O(1): O(n) time, O(n) space.

followUps:
Write the brute-force recursion first; whatever arguments change from one call to the next are your state.

  1. Code the "try every choice" recursion and ignore speed.
  2. List its parameters. For House Robber it is just the index i, so the state is dp[i].
  3. If the answer for the rest still depends on something from the past, add that thing as a dimension. Stock trading with a cooldown needs dp[i][holding], because "do I own a share?" changes what I may do next.
  4. If nothing works, change the meaning: "best answer ending exactly at i" (as in longest increasing subsequence) often works where "best in the first i" does not.

Then check the count: states × work per state must fit the limits, e.g. 104 × 104 = 108 is the upper edge.

Test it in three ways: fill a tiny table by hand, compare against a slow brute force on many small random inputs, and try the edge cases.

  • By hand. House Robber on [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] should give the table 0, 2, 7, 11, 11, 12. Print the real table and compare cell by cell; the first cell that differs points at the bug.
  • Brute force. Try all 2n subsets for n ≤ 8 and compare with the DP on a few thousand random arrays.
  • Edges. Empty input (0), one element ([5] gives 5), all zeros, an impossible target (coin change must return −1, not a huge number), and the largest input for overflow and time.

The hand table costs minutes; the random test is O(tests × 2n) and runs in well under a second.

code.title: Climbing Stairs: group every sequence by its last move
code.python:
end_with = [0, 0, 0]   # end_with[1] and end_with[2] count sequences by last move


# Brute force: build every sequence of 1-steps and 2-steps that sums to n.
def walk(remaining, last_step):
    if remaining == 0:
        end_with[last_step] += 1          # group by last move
        return
    if remaining >= 1:
        walk(remaining - 1, 1)
    if remaining >= 2:
        walk(remaining - 2, 2)


n = 5
# DP: ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2]
ways = [0] * (n + 1)
ways[0] = 1
ways[1] = 1
for i in range(2, n + 1):
    ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2]

walk(n, 0)
print("n = " + str(n))
print("sequences whose last move is 1 step:  " + str(end_with[1]) + "  (ways(" + str(n - 1) + ") = " + str(ways[n - 1]) + ")")
print("sequences whose last move is 2 steps: " + str(end_with[2]) + "  (ways(" + str(n - 2) + ") = " + str(ways[n - 2]) + ")")
# The two groups share nothing and cover everything, so we just add.
print("total by listing = " + str(end_with[1] + end_with[2]) + ", ways(" + str(n) + ") by DP = " + str(ways[n]))
# DP: O(n) time, O(n) space. Listing: about 1.6^n time.

followUps:
Add up one term for each allowed step size: ways[i] = sum of ways[i − s] for every s in S with s ≤ i.

The same "group by the last move" argument holds: a sequence ends with exactly one step s, so the groups do not overlap.

ways[0] = 1;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    for (int s : S)
        if (s <= i) ways[i] += ways[i - s];

Example with S = {1, 3, 5} and n = 5: ways = 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. The last value is ways[4] + ways[2] + ways[0] = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5.

Time O(n × |S|), space O(n). The loop order here counts ordered sequences, which is what a staircase needs.

Set the number of ways for every broken stair to 0 and leave the rest of the recurrence unchanged.

A broken stair cannot be stood on, so no valid sequence passes through it; a 0 there automatically stops it from feeding later stairs.

ways[0] = 1;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    if (broken[i]) { ways[i] = 0; continue; }
    ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + (i >= 2 ? ways[i - 2] : 0);
}

Example: n = 5 with stair 3 broken gives ways = 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2, so the answer is 2 instead of 8 (the two routes are 1+1+2+1 and 2+2+1).

Time O(n), space O(n) for the table plus a set or boolean array for the broken stairs. If the top stair itself is broken the answer is 0.

code.title: Coin change: greedy vs DP on {1, 3, 4} and {1, 5, 10, 25}
code.python:
# Greedy: always take the biggest coin that still fits (coins sorted ascending).
def greedy(coins, amount):
    used = 0
    for c in reversed(coins):
        used += amount // c
        amount %= c
    return used


# DP: dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a = 1 + min over every possible last coin.
def dp_coins(coins, amount):
    INF = 1000000
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        dp[a] = INF
        for c in coins:
            if a >= c:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - c])
    return dp[amount]


odd = [1, 3, 4]
print("coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6")
print("  greedy = " + str(greedy(odd, 6)) + " coins, DP = " + str(dp_coins(odd, 6)) + " coins")
us = [1, 5, 10, 25]
print("coins = [1, 5, 10, 25], amount = 63")
print("  greedy = " + str(greedy(us, 63)) + " coins, DP = " + str(dp_coins(us, 63)) + " coins")
# Greedy: O(coins) time. DP: O(amount * coins) time, O(amount) space.

followUps:
You show that any best answer can hold only a few small coins, so few that it is forced to use as many quarters as greedy does, and then repeat the argument for dimes and nickels.

Swap rules that never make things worse: 5 pennies become 1 nickel, 2 nickels become 1 dime, 3 dimes become 1 quarter + 1 nickel, and 2 dimes + 1 nickel become 1 quarter. So a best answer has at most 4 pennies, 1 nickel and 2 dimes, and not 2 dimes together with a nickel. The most the non-quarter coins can add up to is 10 + 10 + 4 = 24 cents, which is less than 25. So the quarters must cover everything except a remainder under 25, exactly like greedy.

Example: 63 = 25 + 25 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, 6 coins. A machine check also works: compare greedy with DP for every amount below 25 + 10 = 35.

Remember which coin was used last for each amount while filling the table, then walk backwards from the target subtracting those coins.

  1. When 1 + dp[a − c] beats dp[a], store last[a] = c.
  2. After the fill, if dp[amount] is still "infinity" there is no answer.
  3. Otherwise repeat: output last[a], then a −= last[a], until a is 0.
if (1 + dp[a - c] < dp[a]) { dp[a] = 1 + dp[a - c]; last[a] = c; }
...
for (int a = amount; a > 0; a -= last[a])
    result.add(last[a]);

Example: coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: last[6] = 3, last[3] = 3, so the coins are 3, 3.

Time stays O(amount × coins); the extra array is O(amount) and the walk back is at most dp[amount] steps.

code.title: Same transition, two loop orders: combinations vs sequences
code.python:
coins = [1, 2, 5]
amount = 5
print("coins = [1, 2, 5], amount = " + str(amount))

# LC 518: coins in the OUTER loop. Each coin is added in a fixed order,
# so 1+2 and 2+1 are built only once (combinations).
comb = [0] * (amount + 1)
comb[0] = 1
for c in coins:
    for a in range(c, amount + 1):
        comb[a] += comb[a - c]

# LC 377: amounts in the OUTER loop. Any coin can be the last one,
# so 1+2 and 2+1 are counted separately (ordered sequences).
seq = [0] * (amount + 1)
seq[0] = 1
for a in range(1, amount + 1):
    for c in coins:
        if a >= c:
            seq[a] += seq[a - c]

print("combinations (coins outer, LC 518) = " + str(comb[amount]))
print("sequences    (amount outer, LC 377) = " + str(seq[amount]))
# Both: O(amount * coins) time, O(amount) space.

followUps:
The combinations version is really a table with one row per coin; the sequences version has no coin dimension at all, only one row of amounts.

LC 518: dp[i][a] = dp[i−1][a] + dp[i][a−c], meaning "do not use coin i" plus "use it at least once". For coins {1, 2} and amount 3:

coins allowed0123
{1}1111
{1, 2}1122

Answer 2 (1+1+1 and 1+2). The 1D code is this table with rows overwritten in place.

LC 377: dp[a] = sum of dp[a−c] over all coins: 1, 1, 2, 3. Answer 3 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1). No row index means no fixed coin order, so orderings count separately. Both cost O(amount × coins).

Keep the coins in the outer loop, but run the amounts from high to low, so each coin can be added to a sum only once.

Going downward, ways[a − c] is still the value from before coin c was considered, so c is never counted twice in one sum. This is the 0/1 knapsack direction.

ways[0] = 1;
for (int c : coins)
    for (int a = amount; a >= c; a--)
        ways[a] += ways[a - c];

Example: coins {1, 2, 3}, amount 3. After coin 1: ways = 1, 1, 0, 0. After coin 2: 1, 1, 1, 1. After coin 3: 1, 1, 1, 2. Answer 2: {3} and {1, 2}. With the upward loop it would be 3, because 1+1+1 sneaks in.

Time O(amount × coins), space O(amount).

code.title: 0/1 knapsack: 2D table, 1D array and the chosen items
code.python:
w = [1, 3, 4, 5]
v = [1, 4, 5, 7]
n, W = len(w), 7
print("weights = [1, 3, 4, 5], values = [1, 4, 5, 7], capacity = 7")

# 2D: dp[i][c] = best value using the first i items with capacity c.
dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for c in range(W + 1):
        dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]                       # skip item i
        if c >= w[i - 1]:                             # or take it once
            dp[i][c] = max(dp[i][c], dp[i - 1][c - w[i - 1]] + v[i - 1])
print("2D table answer = " + str(dp[n][W]))

# 1D: go from W down, so one[c - w] is still the previous row.
one = [0] * (W + 1)
for i in range(n):
    for c in range(W, w[i] - 1, -1):
        one[c] = max(one[c], one[c - w[i]] + v[i])
print("1D array answer = " + str(one[W]))

# Walk back through the 2D table: a change between rows means "taken".
c = W
for i in range(n, 0, -1):
    if dp[i][c] != dp[i - 1][c]:
        print("took item " + str(i - 1) + " (weight " + str(w[i - 1]) + ", value " + str(v[i - 1]) + ")")
        c -= w[i - 1]
# Time O(n * W). Space O(n * W) for 2D, O(W) for 1D.

followUps:
Because the running time grows with the size of the number W, not with how many digits it takes to write W down.

The input stores W in about log2 W bits. O(n × W) written in terms of those bits b is O(n × 2b), which is exponential. Adding one bit to W doubles the work.

Example with n = 100 items: W = 106 (20 bits) needs 108 steps, about a second. W = 109 needs only 10 more bits to write down, but 1011 steps and a table of 109 cells. The input barely grew; the work grew 1000 times.

A truly polynomial algorithm would be polynomial in n and log W. None is known, since 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard.

Stop indexing the table by capacity and index it by total value instead, as long as the values are small.

  1. Let minW[x] = the lightest weight that gives total value exactly x. Start with minW[0] = 0 and the rest "infinity".
  2. For each item, loop x downward: minW[x] = min(minW[x], minW[x − v] + w).
  3. The answer is the largest x with minW[x] ≤ W.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int x = sumV; x >= v[i]; x--)
        minW[x] = Math.min(minW[x], minW[x - v[i]] + w[i]);

With 100 items of value at most 1000 the table has 105 cells, so about 107 steps instead of 1011. Time O(n × sumV), space O(sumV). If values are huge too, use meet-in-the-middle for n ≤ 40 (about 220 subsets per half) or an approximation.

code.title: 0/1 vs unbounded knapsack: only the loop direction changes
code.python:
w = [1, 3, 4]
v = [15, 50, 60]
W = 8
print("weights = [1, 3, 4], values = [15, 50, 60], capacity = 8")

# 0/1: capacity goes DOWN, so dp[c - w] has not used this item yet.
once = [0] * (W + 1)
for i in range(len(w)):
    for c in range(W, w[i] - 1, -1):
        once[c] = max(once[c], once[c - w[i]] + v[i])

# Unbounded: capacity goes UP, so dp[c - w] may already include this item.
many = [0] * (W + 1)
for i in range(len(w)):
    for c in range(w[i], W + 1):
        many[c] = max(many[c], many[c - w[i]] + v[i])

print("0/1 knapsack (each item once)  = " + str(once[W]))
print("unbounded (items can repeat)   = " + str(many[W]))
# The only change is the direction of the inner loop.
# Both: O(n * W) time, O(W) space.

followUps:
Split each item's k copies into a few bundles of sizes 1, 2, 4, … plus a remainder, and then run the normal 0/1 knapsack on the bundles.

Any count from 0 to k can be built by choosing some of these bundles, so nothing is lost, and there are only about log2 k bundles instead of k copies.

Example: k = 13 becomes bundles of 1, 2, 4 and 6 copies (1 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 13). To take 11 copies, pick 1 + 4 + 6. A bundle of 4 copies is one 0/1 item with weight 4w and value 4v.

Time O(W × sum of log k) instead of O(W × sum of k), space O(W). For k = 1000 that is 10 bundles per item instead of 1000. A sliding-window maximum per remainder class of w gets O(n × W), but is rarely needed in interviews.

No. For the best value, items-outer and capacity-outer give the same answer; only the inner direction (capacity going up) matters.

A maximum does not care in which order the items were put into the bag: the bag {3, 3, 1, 1} has the same value however you arrange it. Loop order only matters when you count, because then the two orders decide whether 1+2 and 2+1 are one way or two.

Example: weights {1, 3, 4}, values {15, 50, 60}, capacity 8. Items outer gives 130. Capacity outer, dp[c] = max over items of dp[c − w] + v, also gives 130 (two of weight 3, two of weight 1).

Both are O(n × W) time and O(W) space. For 0/1 knapsack in 1D the items must stay in the outer loop, otherwise an item can be reused.

code.title: LCS: fill the table, then walk back to get the string
code.python:
a, b = "ABCBDAB", "BDCABA"
n, m = len(a), len(b)
print("a = " + a + ", b = " + b)

# dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i chars of a and first j chars of b.
dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
            dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
        else:
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])

# Walk back from the bottom-right corner to collect the characters.
out = []
i, j = n, m
while i > 0 and j > 0:
    if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:              # match: keep it, go diagonal
        out.append(a[i - 1])
        i -= 1
        j -= 1
    elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:    # otherwise follow the larger side
        i -= 1
    else:
        j -= 1
out.reverse()                             # collected back to front
print("LCS length = " + str(dp[n][m]))
print("one LCS    = " + "".join(out))
print("table cells kept = " + str((n + 1) * (m + 1)))
# Time O(n * m). Space O(n * m): the walk back needs the whole table.

followUps:
Do the same walk back from the corner, but when up and left tie, follow both branches, and collect the finished strings in a set to remove duplicates.

  1. At (i, j): if the characters match, add the character and go diagonal.
  2. Otherwise go up if dp[i−1][j] == dp[i][j], and also go left if dp[i][j−1] == dp[i][j].
  3. At i = 0 or j = 0, reverse what you collected and add it to the set.

Example: "ABCBDAB" and "BDCABA" have length 4 and three different answers: BCBA, BCAB and BDAB.

The table is still O(n × m), but the number of answers can grow exponentially, so the output alone can be huge. Memoizing the set of strings per cell (i, j) avoids walking the same cell many times.

Then it turns into the longest increasing subsequence problem, which runs in O(n log n) instead of O(n × m).

  1. Record the position of every character in the string with distinct characters, A.
  2. Replace each character of B by its position in A; drop characters that A does not have.
  3. A common subsequence must go left to right in both strings, so it is exactly an increasing run of these positions. Find the longest one with the binary-search method.

Example: A = "abcde" (a=0, b=1, c=2, d=3, e=4), B = "badce" gives positions 1, 0, 3, 2, 4. The longest increasing run has length 3, for example 0, 2, 4 = "ace".

Time O(m log n), space O(n + m). With lengths of 105 this is about 2 × 106 steps instead of 1010.

code.title: Edit distance: full table vs one row with a saved diagonal
code.python:
# Full table: dp[i][j] = edits to turn the first i chars of a into the first j of b.
def full(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n + 1):
        dp[i][0] = i                      # delete everything
    for j in range(m + 1):
        dp[0][j] = j                      # insert everything
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            same = 0 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] else 1
            dp[i][j] = min(dp[i - 1][j - 1] + same,   # keep or replace
                           dp[i - 1][j] + 1,          # delete
                           dp[i][j - 1] + 1)          # insert
    return dp[n][m]


# One row: 'diag' saves the old dp[i-1][j-1] before it is overwritten.
def one_row(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    row = list(range(m + 1))
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        diag = row[0]
        row[0] = i
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            up = row[j]
            same = 0 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] else 1
            row[j] = min(diag + same, up + 1, row[j - 1] + 1)
            diag = up
    return row[m]


tests = [("horse", "ros"), ("intention", "execution")]
for s, t in tests:
    print(s + " -> " + t + ": full table = " + str(full(s, t)) + ", one row = " + str(one_row(s, t)))
# Time O(n * m) for both. Space O(n * m) vs O(m).

followUps:
Add a fourth case to the minimum: if the last two characters of both prefixes are the same pair in swapped order, you may fix both with one swap.

if (i > 1 && j > 1
    && a[i-1] == b[j-2] && a[i-2] == b[j-1])
    dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i-2][j-2] + 1);

Example: "ab" to "ba" is 2 with plain edit distance (two replaces) and 1 with the swap. "form" to "from" also drops from 2 to 1.

Time stays O(n × m). The new case reads row i − 2, so the space-saving version must keep three rows instead of one row plus a diagonal value. This simple form is called optimal string alignment: it never edits the same piece twice. The full Damerau distance needs an extra table of last positions per character.

They do not run edit distance against every word; they first use an index to pull out a small list of likely candidates and only then check those few exactly.

  • n-gram index: store every 3-letter piece of each word. "hello" and "helo" share "hel", so a lookup on the query's pieces finds nearby words quickly.
  • Delete dictionary (SymSpell): pre-store each word with up to 2 letters deleted; delete letters from the query the same way and look up directly.
  • Levenshtein automaton: build a small machine that accepts all strings within distance k of the query and walk it together with the sorted term dictionary (Lucene does this).

The survivors are verified with the banded DP, O(n × k), with k usually 1 or 2, and then ranked by how common each word is. A dictionary of 106 words is cut to a few dozen candidates per query.

code.title: Subset sum: boolean table vs a 64-bit bitset
code.python:
def yes_no(x):
    return "yes" if x else "no"


nums = [3, 4, 12, 5, 2, 20]
limit = 63                                # sums 0..63 fit in one 64-bit word
print("nums = [3, 4, 12, 5, 2, 20]")

# Classic boolean table: one array cell per sum.
can = [False] * (limit + 1)
can[0] = True
for x in nums:
    for s in range(limit, x - 1, -1):
        if can[s - x]:
            can[s] = True

# Bitset: bit s of 'bits' is 1 when sum s is reachable.
# Shifting left by x adds x to every reachable sum at once.
bits = 1
for x in nums:
    bits |= bits << x

for t in [9, 30, 45, 47]:
    print("sum " + str(t) + ": table says " + yes_no(can[t])
          + ", bitset says " + yes_no((bits >> t) & 1 == 1))
print("memory: table = " + str(limit + 1) + " cells, bitset = 1 word of 64 bits")
# Table: O(n * S) time, O(S) cells. Bitset: O(n * S / 64) time, S / 64 words.

followUps:
Rolling loses information whenever you need more than the final number, most often when you must rebuild the actual path, string or item list.

The walk back asks "which neighbour did this cell come from?" for cells in old rows, and those rows were overwritten. It also fails if a transition reaches further back than the rows you kept, for example Damerau's swap reads row i − 2 while you kept only row i − 1.

Example: LCS of "ABCBDAB" and "BDCABA". Two rows of 7 cells give the length 4, but not the string "BCBA", which needs all 8 × 7 = 56 cells.

Fixes: keep only 1 choice bit per cell (n × m / 8 bytes instead of 4 × n × m), or use Hirschberg's divide & conquer, which rebuilds the answer in O(n + m) space for about twice the time.

Put i in the top 32 bits and j in the bottom 32 bits of one 64-bit integer.

long key = ((long) i << 32) | (j & 0xFFFFFFFFL);
int i2 = (int) (key >>> 32);   // unpack
int j2 = (int) key;

Example: i = 3, j = 5 gives 3 × 232 + 5 = 12884901893, and unpacking returns 3 and 5. The cast to long before the shift is essential; without it the shift happens in 32 bits and i is lost. The mask stops a negative j from filling the top half with 1s.

If you know the number of columns, key = (long) i * cols + j is simpler and gives denser keys. Both are O(1) and avoid creating a pair object per lookup, which makes a hash-map memo several times faster and smaller. In JS use a number as i * cols + j while it stays below 253.

code.title: Unique Paths II fills forward, Dungeon Game fills backward
code.python:
# Unique Paths II: 1 = obstacle. Fill FORWARD: ways depend on cells above/left.
grid = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
R, C = 3, 3
ways = [[0] * C for _ in range(R)]
for r in range(R):
    for c in range(C):
        if grid[r][c] == 1:
            ways[r][c] = 0
        elif r == 0 and c == 0:
            ways[r][c] = 1
        else:
            up = ways[r - 1][c] if r > 0 else 0
            left = ways[r][c - 1] if c > 0 else 0
            ways[r][c] = up + left
print("obstacle grid = [[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]]")
print("unique paths (filled forward) = " + str(ways[R - 1][C - 1]))

# Dungeon Game: fill BACKWARD: need[r][c] = least health when entering the cell.
d = [[-2, -3, 3], [-5, -10, 1], [10, 30, -5]]
BIG = 1000000000
need = [[BIG] * (C + 1) for _ in range(R + 1)]
need[R][C - 1] = 1                        # border next to the goal: leave with 1 health
need[R - 1][C] = 1
for r in range(R - 1, -1, -1):
    for c in range(C - 1, -1, -1):
        nxt = min(need[r + 1][c], need[r][c + 1])     # cheaper way onward
        need[r][c] = max(1, nxt - d[r][c])            # never below 1
print("dungeon = [[-2,-3,3],[-5,-10,1],[10,30,-5]]")
print("minimum starting health (filled backward) = " + str(need[0][0]))
# Both: O(R * C) time and space.

followUps:
Yes, it works, because if a starting health H survives then every larger H survives too; it is just slower than the backward DP.

Once H is fixed, the forward problem has a single number per cell again: the most health you can have on arriving there. Fill it left to right, top to bottom, treating a cell as unreachable if health would drop to 0 or below. H is good if the last cell is reachable.

Example on the classic grid [[−2,−3,3],[−5,−10,1],[10,30,−5]]: H = 6 fails (the route right, right, down, down hits 0 at the last room) and H = 7 passes, so the answer is 7.

Cost: O(R × C) per check times about log2(sum of the damage) ≈ 30 checks, against a single O(R × C) pass for the backward DP. It is a good fallback when you cannot see the backward state.

Then the simple row-by-row DP no longer works, because cells can depend on each other in a circle and there is no fill order; you switch to a shortest-path algorithm on the grid graph.

With moves only right and down, every cell depends on cells that are already final. With 4 directions, A may be reached from B and B from A.

  • Fewest steps: BFS, O(R × C).
  • Smallest path sum with non-negative costs: Dijkstra with a heap, O(R × C × log(R × C)).
  • Negative cells: Bellman-Ford, and the answer may be unbounded if you can loop through a positive-gain cycle.
  • Counting paths: infinite unless revisits are banned, and then it needs backtracking, which is exponential.

Example: in [[1, 9, 1], [1, 9, 1], [1, 1, 1]] the cheapest route to the top-right cell goes down, across and back up: cost 7, not 11.

code.title: Knapsack with capacity 10^9: index the table by value
code.python:
w = [400000000, 300000000, 500000000, 600000000]
v = [4, 5, 7, 8]
W = 1000000000
print("weights = [400000000, 300000000, 500000000, 600000000]")
print("values  = [4, 5, 7, 8], capacity = 1000000000")

# A table indexed by capacity would need 10^9 cells. Index by VALUE instead:
# min_w[x] = smallest total weight that reaches value exactly x.
total = sum(v)
INF = float("inf")
min_w = [INF] * (total + 1)
min_w[0] = 0
for i in range(len(w)):
    for x in range(total, v[i] - 1, -1):          # downward: each item once
        if min_w[x - v[i]] != INF:
            min_w[x] = min(min_w[x], min_w[x - v[i]] + w[i])

# Answer: the largest value whose lightest weight still fits.
best = 0
for x in range(total + 1):
    if min_w[x] <= W:
        best = x
print("best value = " + str(best) + " (weight used = " + str(min_w[best]) + ")")
print("table size = " + str(total + 1) + " cells instead of 1000000001")
# Time O(n * sum of values), space O(sum of values).

followUps:
Shrink every value by the same factor, so the value-indexed table becomes small, and accept a small, controlled error from the rounding.

  1. Pick K = ε × vmax / n.
  2. Replace each value by floor(v / K). Now every value is at most n / ε.
  3. Run the "lightest weight for each value" DP on the small values and return the items it picks.

Example: values 1234, 5678, 9012 with n = 3 and ε = 0.3 give K ≈ 901, and the scaled values are 1, 6, 10. The table needs 18 cells instead of about 16000.

Rounding loses less than K per item, so at most n × K = ε × vmax in total, and vmax ≤ best answer (assuming every item fits alone). So the result is at least (1 − ε) × best. Time O(n3 / ε): polynomial in both n and 1/ε.

Parallelise inside one item's row, not across items: every cell of row i reads only row i − 1, so all capacities can be computed at the same time.

  1. Keep two arrays, prev and cur (the in-place backward trick creates a dependency on write order, so drop it).
  2. Split the range 0..W into one chunk per thread; each thread computes cur[c] = max(prev[c], prev[c − w] + v) for its chunk.
  3. Swap the arrays and go to the next item. Items stay sequential.

Example: W = 108 on 8 cores gives chunks of 1.25 × 107 cells. The loop is also easy for SIMD or a GPU. Work stays O(n × W); time drops to about O(n × W / p), limited in practice by memory speed. For yes/no subset sum, a bitset shift already handles 64 cells per instruction.

code.title: Stress test: a DP against brute force on random inputs
code.python:
seed = 7


# Tiny random generator, so every run produces the same tests.
def nxt(bound):
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed % bound


# Slow but obviously right: try every subset with no two neighbours.
def brute(a):
    best = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(a)):
        if mask & (mask << 1):            # two neighbours chosen
            continue
        total = sum(a[i] for i in range(len(a)) if mask >> i & 1)
        best = max(best, total)
    return best


# The DP under test (House Robber). 'buggy' drops the "skip this house" option.
def dp(a, buggy):
    prev2, prev1 = 0, 0
    for x in a:
        cur = prev2 + x if buggy else max(prev1, prev2 + x)
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, cur
    return max(prev1, prev2)


tests, bad_good, bad_buggy, first = 500, 0, 0, ""
for t in range(tests):
    size = nxt(7)                         # small sizes, 0 to 6
    a = [nxt(10) for _ in range(size)]
    want = brute(a)
    if dp(a, False) != want:
        bad_good += 1
    if dp(a, True) != want:
        if bad_buggy == 0:
            text = "".join(str(x) + " " for x in a)
            first = "[ " + text + "] expected " + str(want) + ", got " + str(dp(a, True))
        bad_buggy += 1
print("random tests = " + str(tests))
print("correct DP mismatches = " + str(bad_good))
print("buggy DP mismatches   = " + str(bad_buggy))
print("first failing input for the buggy DP: " + first)
# Each test: brute force O(2^n * n), DP O(n). Small n keeps it fast.

followUps:
Keep most tests tiny, so the brute force is instant and a failure is short enough to read, and add a few large ones only for speed and overflow.

  • Size: n from 0 to about 8. Brute force over 28 = 256 subsets is free, and 0, 1 and 2 hit the base cases often.
  • Values: a narrow range such as 0 to 9, so ties, duplicates and zeros appear all the time. With values up to 109 two equal elements almost never occur and tie-breaking bugs stay hidden.
  • Targets: include ones that cannot be reached.
  • Large runs: a few inputs at the maximum size without brute force, to check time, memory and overflow.

Example: 500 arrays of length 0 to 6 with digits 0 to 9 expose a missing max in House Robber on a 3-element array such as [8, 9, 0]. Fix the random seed so a failure can be replayed.

Assert the facts that must be true for every cell if the recurrence is right, so a wrong loop bound or base case fails loudly at the cell where it happens.

  • Range: LCS has 0 ≤ dp[i][j] ≤ min(i, j); edit distance is at most max(i, j); a count is never negative (a negative count means overflow).
  • Monotone: knapsack dp[i][c] ≥ dp[i−1][c] and dp[i][c] ≥ dp[i][c−1]: more items or more room never hurts.
  • Small steps: neighbouring LCS or edit-distance cells differ by at most 1.
  • Sentinels: never add to "infinity"; assert dp[a − c] != INF before + 1.
  • Indexes: c − w ≥ 0 before every read.
  • Answer: the rebuilt solution, re-scored from scratch, equals the DP value.

Example: knapsack row 3 showing 9 at capacity 6 and 8 at capacity 7 breaks the monotone rule at once. The checks are O(1) per cell and can be switched off in production.
